chapter_theme: Songs at Vadathirumullaivayil (வடதிருமுல்லைவாயில்): the poet asks whether grace will leave him long in darkness, confesses courtesans who take a man home by a trick and rob him, and asks not to fall into the snare of women's eyes; the praise names Murugan as Siva's guru, the Goddess of the burning ground, and Siva the Masilamani who defeated Kali.
structure_note: A plea for grace (682), a courtesan song (683) and a song on women's eyes (684). Song 682 is badly garbled.

682.reading: The poet, calling himself without understanding, asks whether Murugan has the grace to remove his distress so he may reach the shore of this sea-girt earth, whether he will leave him long in the house of darkness, whether there is no grace for him, for he does not know what is fitting, and when the day will come that ends the hut of the body. The praise is a tangle of names: the Goddess at Arunachala, Murugan as Siva-guru, the son of Parameswari who plays with ghosts in the cactus forest of the burning ground, the nephew of Vishnu, the son of the one who danced at Thillai, at Vadamullaivayil of jasmine groves.
682.nuance: The plea is a series of anxious questions (அருள்வல்லையோ, இடுமோ, அருளில்லையோ). குடில் இல்லமே தரு நாள் எது may ask when the body-hut will cease to be given, that is, when birth ends; the reading is tentative. Many words of the praise (குணவல்வா, பரிசெல்ரவி, மோடமடர்) look garbled.

683.reading: The poet describes women with moonlike faces who face men coming from afar, flirt, fall on their shoulders as if old lovers, take them home by a trick, give their lips while they plunder the wealth, then fall silent and pick quarrels, and asks whether he, a fool and sinner whose mind has failed in delusion for these deceitful wanton women, will gain salvation. The praise names the vel thrown from the peacock at Sura, the nephew of Krishna who climbed the mortar to steal butter from the hanging pots in the herders' villages, and Siva the Masilamani, the first Lord who defeated Kali in contest and whose dancing feet the sea king, Brahma and Vishnu worship.
683.nuance: The courtesan's cycle is told in order: approach, false intimacy (முன்னாளில் இணங்கிய மாதர் போல்), a trick to bring him home, plunder while the lips are given, then silence and quarrels. மாசிலாமணி is the name of the Siva of Thirumullaivayil.

684.reading: The poet asks that he not fall into the snare of women who walk the street outdoing swans and peacocks, speak like cuckoos and shoot eye-arrows like Kama, false maidens with jewelled breasts, but that Murugan rule him in joy through the snare of loving knowledge of his feet, without the evil eye. The praise names Murugan the guru of the father who wears the crescent, vanni, serpent and konrai, the nephew of Rama whose arrow sent Ravana's heads to the sky, the vel that made the mountain leap, and the lord of supreme knowledge at northern Mullaivayil where sages do penance.
684.nuance: கண்ணி is played twice: the women's snare (கண்ணியில் விழாமல்) and a 'snare' of knowledge of the feet (பதஞான கண்ணியில்), so the remedy is a better binding. கண்ணுறு வராமல் may mean free of the evil eye. சொல்லுமுனிவோர் தவம்புரி names sages doing penance at the shrine.

links.note: Both warn that the courtesan's sweet words serve her wish for wealth; 683 shows the words in action, the talk of old intimacy leading to the house where the wealth is plundered.

The poet, calling himself without understanding (அறிவில்லியாம் அடியேன்), asks anxiously whether grace will leave him long in the house of darkness (நெடுநாள் இருள் இல்லிலே இடுமோ, அருளில்லையோ). Tirumular says the soul born and dying through folly (பேதைமையாலே) finds its many darknesses go at the ripe season for joining Siva's grace (சிவனருள் சேர்பருவத்து), once it has renounced. Tirumular names the condition and timing the poet's questions leave open.

The Naladiyar's worthless woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from the hand, then lies down like a balking ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு சேமாபோல் குப்புறூஉம்). The song's women give their lips while they plunder the wealth (கனிவாய் அதரந்தரு நாளிலே பொருள் சூறைகள் கொண்டு), then fall silent and pick quarrels (மோனமாய் ... சண்டைகள்). Both give the same three-step cycle of sweetness, taking and turning away.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). The song asks not to fall into the women's snare (கண்ணியில் விழாமல்) but to be held within the snare of knowledge of the feet (பதஞான கண்ணியிலுளாக). Both answer a binding with a better binding rather than with none.

source_issues: Song 682: several words look garbled (குணவல் வாசிவனே, பரிசெல்ரவி, மோடமடர், நகாகன), and the praise is hard to read.
